explain.body: The family of hydrocarbons constitutes a very large number of simple organic compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only. This means that a hydrocarbon has carbon and hydrogen atoms and no other elements.

explain.body: Carbon forms four covalent bonds. Its ability to link to itself is called catenation. Carbon can therefore form long, straight and branched chains and rings, which gives many possible structures.

explain.title: What makes an alkane?
explain.body: Alkanes are the simplest family of hydrocarbons with only carbon – carbon and carbon – hydrogen single bond. Alkanes are also called saturated hydrocarbons because all the four valencies of carbon in them are fully utilized either by hydrogen atoms or by other carbon atoms. Their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, where n is an integer.

explain.title: The parts of an IUPAC name
explain.body: Root: It tells us the number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain present in the molecule. Suffix: It is added after the root and tells us about the class of organic compounds. Prefix: It is indicated before the root and tells us about the group or groups attached to the longest chain. For an alkane, the suffix is -ane.

explain.title: Roots to remember
explain.body: Meth- means 1 carbon, eth- 2, prop- 3, but- 4, pent- 5, hex- 6, hept- 7, oct- 8, non- 9 and dec- 10. Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon and is also called the parent hydrocarbon.

explain.title: How to name a branched alkane
explain.body: Choose the longest continuous chain. Number it from the end closest to a branch, name the branch as a prefix, and attach its position number. For example, the four-carbon chain in CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH₂—CH₃ gives the name 2-methylbutane.

explain.title: Alkane structures
explain.body: A methyl group is CH₃ and a methylene group is CH₂. In a straight-chain alkane, the end carbon atoms are usually CH₃ groups, while the carbon atoms in the middle are CH₂ groups.

mistakes: Do not choose a shorter chain just because it looks like the main horizontal line; find the longest continuous carbon chain.
Do not number from the end farther from the branch; use the nearest end to give the lowest possible branch number.
Do not forget the locant (position number) before a branch name, such as 2-methylbutane.
Do not use an alkene suffix such as -ene for an alkane; alkanes take the suffix -ane.
Do not confuse a methyl group, CH₃, with a methylene group, CH₂.

explain.title: Cracking higher hydrocarbons
explain.body: Cracking is the name of a process in which hydrocarbons with higher molecular masses (which are lesser in demand) are broken up into smaller hydrocarbons which are more in demand. This is done by heating the hydrocarbons at high temperature in the presence of a catalyst. Naphtha is heated at around 500°C with zeolite to give hydrocarbons with five to ten carbon atoms.

explain.title: Reducing alkenes and alkynes
explain.body: Alkanes can be prepared by reducing alkenes and alkynes with hydrogen gas in the presence of nickel metal as a catalyst. Methane cannot be prepared by this method. The reaction is also called hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes and is an example of addition reaction. An addition reaction occurs when hydrogen (H₂) is added to an unsaturated compound.

explain.title: Reducing alkyl halides
explain.body: Alkyl halides (R-X) can be reduced to alkanes with hydrogen generated by reaction of zinc metal with hydrochloric acid. The textbook represents this hydrogen as [2H]: R—X + [2H] → R—H + H—X.

notes.title: Important Reactions of Alkanes
notes.answer: The two important reactions are halogenation (substitution) and combustion.
notes.explanation: Alkanes are mostly unreactive, but your textbook describes two important reactions: halogenation and combustion. Halogenation replaces hydrogen atoms with halogen atoms in UV light. Combustion burns an alkane in oxygen to form carbon dioxide, water and heat.

steps: In halogenation, a halogen replaces a hydrogen atom in an alkane.
UV light is used, so this is called photochemical substitution.
In combustion, an alkane reacts with oxygen to form CO₂ and H₂O, releasing heat.
Methane reacts with chlorine to form chloromethane and hydrogen chloride.

notes.title: Hydrocarbons and alkanes
notes.answer: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes have carbon–carbon single bonds and undergo combustion, substitution and cracking reactions.
notes.explanation: Hydrocarbons are compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with single bonds between their carbon atoms. Their reactions and physical properties depend on their structure and size.
notes.simple: Hydrocarbons contain carbon and hydrogen only. When they burn completely, they produce carbon dioxide, water and heat.
examples: Methane (CH₄) is the main component of natural gas.
Complete combustion of propane produces carbon dioxide and water.
